title: Classes, constructors and operator overloading
subtitle: Put the data behind a wall and let the methods guard it.

cls.title: Defining a class
cls.body: Members are private by default in a class (public in a struct). Keep data private and offer public methods: the class can then enforce rules (balance never negative) that raw data cannot. Watch the guard in action — the negative deposit is ignored.

ctor.title: Constructors and destructors
ctor.body: A constructor has the class name, no return type, and runs when an object is created — use it (and the initialiser list) to put the object in a valid state. A destructor ~Name() runs when it is destroyed: close files, free memory. A copy constructor builds a new object from an existing one; if the class owns a raw pointer, copy the pointed data (deep copy), not just the pointer.

this.title: this, static and const
this.body: this is a pointer to the current object. A static member belongs to the class, shared by all objects (an instance counter). A const method promises not to change the object, so it can be called on const objects.

ovl.title: Operator overloading
ovl.body: C++ lets a class define what + - == << [] mean for it: Vec operator+(const Vec& o) const makes a + b work on vectors. Rules: you cannot invent new operators or change precedence; :: . .* ?: cannot be overloaded; keep the meaning intuitive. The expression a + b is just sugar for a.operator+(b).

friend.title: Friends and stream operators
friend.body: A friend function may touch private members. It is how operator<<(ostream&, const T&) is usually written — the left operand is the stream, not your class, so it cannot be a member. Return the stream to allow chaining: cout << a << b.

conv.title: Conversions
conv.body: A one-argument constructor is an implicit conversion (mark it explicit to stop surprises). A conversion operator operator double() converts out. Use them sparingly: hidden conversions make code harder to read.
